speechtext:

Considering that a $4 million loan in addition to a $1 million subsidy have just been granted to Jamaica for a 30-year period at a 3 per cent rate,
Considering that our government contributes very generously to the development of other countries,

INFLATION-INQUIRY WHETHER GOVERNMENT MADE PROPOSALS TO PROVINCES CONCERNING APPROPRIATE INCREASE IN MONEY SUPPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is addressed to the Acting Minister of Finance. In the documentation sent out during the consensus discussions, would the Acting Minister of Finance indicate if there was any documentation supplied especially to the provinces concerning what the government felt would be a suitable increase in the money supply during the restraint period and if so what percentage increase does the government propose? Is it 4 per cent, 8 per cent or even higher?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (Acting Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: INFLATION-INQUIRY WHETHER GOVERNMENT MADE PROPOSALS TO PROVINCES CONCERNING APPROPRIATE INCREASE IN MONEY SUPPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think this present line of questioning indicates the difficulty of achieving a consensus and conducting negotiations. If the government is to behave intelligently it must make proposals without thereby being bound by them. A variety of proposals have been made to a variety of groups. We are now in the process of getting the reaction of these groups and are trying to synthesize and to resolve the conflicting interests. I do not think it would be particularly helpful to deal in detail in the House at this juncture with the initial proposals made.

subtopic: INFLATION-REASON FOR LARGE INCREASE IN MONEY SUPPLY

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, since the Acting Minister of Finance does not appear to wish to deal with the future, and in view of the fact that the Wood Gundy, May, 1975, publication reviewing the economy states that our money increased by 33 per cent, annualized in the first quarter of this year, compared with 4 per cent in the United States, would the minister indicate why such a staggering increase in our money supply was felt justified in the first quarter of this year?

subtopic: RENT INCREASES FOR SENIOR CITIZEN UNITS-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO PREVENT
RENT INCREASES FOR SENIOR CITIZEN UNITS-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO PREVENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of State for Urban Affairs. Considering that the documents that were sent out to both organized labour and to provinces-which they received last week and which were the only written documents sent out in this exercise, and as far as the provinces and the organized labour movement are concerned it is their understanding these are the only written documents they will get from the government-contain no provisions for dealing with rent increases, would the minister say, in light of the announcement that CMHC will permit an increase in the rent for senior citizens in metro Toronto of between 21 and 59 per cent effective on August 1, whether he has any plans which he intends to implement to head off what could be a disastrous increase in rents for senior citizens in that area?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barney Danson (Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subtopic: RENT INCREASES FOR SENIOR CITIZEN UNITS-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO PREVENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the rental increases to which the hon. member referred are under the limited dividend rental program. These are the only rents to be increased that I know of and they are carefully observed by the corporation to make certain that they reflect only actual increases in operating costs and nothing more. I believe it would be wrong to have one segment of the population paying less and others paying an undue amount more. We are trying to achieve equity in this situation for all Canadians, and these increases reflect actual increases in operating costs.

subtopic: RENT INCREASES FOR SENIOR CITIZEN UNITS-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO PREVENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, just to ensure that I understand what the minister is saying, is he saying that it would be inequitable for the government to take steps specifically to keep down the housing costs of senior citizens, or is he saying that such a selective move would be unfair?

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subtopic: RENT INCREASES FOR SENIOR CITIZEN UNITS-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO PREVENT
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, we do it all the time through senior citizen housing, through section 44(1) of the National Housing Act under which we subsidize those people who need it and where high priority is given to senior citizens, and for those in low income groups this is also done in other ways. In this situation for limited dividend housing, if the rents did not reflect the real increase, no more apartments would be built. The fact is that we have more than double the number of calls for building new rental accommodations at low rates for Canadians as a result of those programs and of keeping the rents low, but allowing them to reflect an actual increase in costs.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED INSTALLATION OF NAVIGATIONAL EQUIPMENT AT VAL D'OR AND ROUYN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the hon. Minister of Transport.
Surely the minister is aware of the very serious problem situation which has existed at both Val d'Or and Rouyn airports ever since the withdrawal of the National Defence component. Air traffic at both these airports is so heavy that it has become a major source of danger for aviation in general. Could the minister advise the House today whether his department is taking the necessary steps to install navigational equipment so as to ensure safety as soon as possible both in Val d'Or and Rouyn?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think I already answered a somewhat similar question last week. Following the removal of the radar station at the military airport, we have sent investigators in the field-they are probably still there-to study the issue of air traffic. If they should report the least possible danger, as suggested by the hon. member, we shall see to it that navigational equipment is in operation to prevent any possible accidents at both these airports.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED INSTALLATION OF NAVIGATIONAL EQUIPMENT AT VAL D'OR AND ROUYN
speechtext:

speechtext:

Many statements have been made since the leader of the Social Credit party asked the minister questions yesterday. Violent crimes are on the increase in Canada, and the minister is blamed for many things, including the housing

situation in Canada, where starts are down 25 per cent. Is the purpose of the extension date of the penalty in reference to capital murder to bring in new legislation to ban capital punishment, or is it to bundle all capital murder convictions-and there may be seven or eight-together and have one political smell at one time?

subsubtopic: REASON FOR POSTPONEMENT OF DEATH PENALTY IN CAPITAL MURDER CASES
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: REASON FOR POSTPONEMENT OF DEATH PENALTY IN CAPITAL MURDER CASES
speechtext:

extension?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it was impossible to deal properly and fully with the question of Mr. Vaillancourt before May 15, the day set for execution. The case was quite complex, and there were implications which went beyond that one particular case. We wanted to consider it in depth.

SUGGESTION SOLICITOR GENERAL POSSIBLY MISLED HOUSE WHEN INTRODUCING LEGISLATION ON CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: Could the minister advise the House if his attitude and philosophy at the time he produced the legislation banning the death penalty for capital murder was the same as the philosophy and attitude he exercises now where he says he will not under any condition agree to having the penalty for capital murder carried out at this time? subtopic: SUGGESTION SOLICITOR GENERAL POSSIBLY MISLED HOUSE WHEN INTRODUCING LEGISLATION ON CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: With the information I now have I am completely opposed to capital punishment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of State for Urban Affairs. Can the minister clarify the statements
May 7, 1975

Oral Questions NATIONAL PARKS
made by this special assistant about the firing of the Toronto Harbourfront chief, Mr. Miskiman, as a result of the unsuccessful attempt to date to develop the 1972 Liberal election campaign promise, which was one of many? Can the minister also tell the House what steps are being taken by his department to bring some semblance of order to the chaotic situation which now exists surrounding this election "goodie"-some goodie it was, too.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barney Danson (Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: TORONTO WATERFRONT PARK-ALLEGED FIRING OF MR. MISKIMAN-REASON FOR INCREASED COST-SUGGESTED CLOSER COOPERATION WITH CITY OFFICIALS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is no chaos. It is only in the mind of one journalist who seemed to have the situation totally confused. Mr. Miskiman is still there and I hope he will continue to be. He is a very able person from the executive exchange program. He is running the show and doing an excellent job and we are behind him 100 per cent. I will meet with the mayor of Toronto on Friday following the regular weekly meeting with the intergovernmental steering committee which meets regularly. There is complete co-operation and understanding between the city, Metro, the province and ourselves and we are producing what will be an excellent program of excellent planning for this park which will be for all time.

subsubtopic: TORONTO WATERFRONT PARK-ALLEGED FIRING OF MR. MISKIMAN-REASON FOR INCREASED COST-SUGGESTED CLOSER COOPERATION WITH CITY OFFICIALS
speechtext: A supplementary, Mr. Speaker. It is obvious there exists a lack of communication within the minister's department. Can the minister explain why the $30 million original estimate for the park has skyrocketed to some $100 million with very little to show for it? I have personally inspected the site, as have many others. Can the minister assure the House that closer consultation will take place with Toronto city officials who have objected that there has not been enough consultation with them in the past?

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: TORONTO WATERFRONT PARK-ALLEGED FIRING OF MR. MISKIMAN-REASON FOR INCREASED COST-SUGGESTED CLOSER COOPERATION WITH CITY OFFICIALS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the elected representatives have not made that objection to me, that there has not been sufficient consultation. Certainly, consultation has been continuing and positive between those people and myself. As I mentioned, I will be meeting with the mayor, to whom I spoke twice in the last couple of weeks, on this subject. There is continuing dialogue and we want to see continued co-operation. As far as the cost of the land is concerned, that is within the province of my colleague, the Minister of Public Works. This is perhaps one of the most valuable sites in Canada and I understand expropriation is proceeding.

subsubtopic: TORONTO WATERFRONT PARK-ALLEGED FIRING OF MR. MISKIMAN-REASON FOR INCREASED COST-SUGGESTED CLOSER COOPERATION WITH CITY OFFICIALS
speechtext: A final short supplementary, Mr. Speaker. Can the minister advise the House why it is taking so long to have any obvious development on the waterfront park when it was promised that the date of completion would be earlier?

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: TORONTO WATERFRONT PARK-ALLEGED FIRING OF MR. MISKIMAN-REASON FOR INCREASED COST-SUGGESTED CLOSER COOPERATION WITH CITY OFFICIALS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I mentioned that this is probably one of the most valuable sites in Canada and that is why we are taking time in the preparation and planning so that the people of Toronto will have a park that is for all time. It should be developed well and I think we should show a considerable amount of forethought. In the meantime, activity is taking place. Over half a million people visited the site last year and that is a lot of people, even for Toronto.

speechtext:
1.	With reference to the implementation of the metric system, what consideration was given to housewives?
2.	What discussions, if any, were held with housewives to assist them in cooking problems, particularly in view of the fact that all recipe books, to date, are not based on the metric system?
3.	Does the government propose to have all recipes for good food rewritten under its auspices and, if so, will it underwrite the cost?
4.	What is the total cost for implementation of the metric system for both the public and private sector?
5.	What other nations in the North American continent are implementing the metric system?

May 7, 1975

6.	What inconveniences will result to the average householder and housewife, landowner, the municipal government, manufacturers, consumers, etc.?
7.	What input has there been by the citizens of Canada to implement the metric system?
8.	What group, if any, requested the change to the metric system at this time when our economy is so strained?
9.	Does any particular group stand to benefit financially by the implementation of the metric system and, if so, which one?
10.	(a) Who is responsible for the educational system to convert to the metric system (b) what action has been taken in this regard and in what way (c) in what locations has such action been taken (d) at what cost?

speakeroldname: Mr. Gaston Clermont (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: METRIC CONVERSION
speechtext:
1. Some of the ways in which housewives are represented in the committee structure of the Metric Commission are through the Consumers' Association of Canada, the Canadian Home Economics Association and the Canadian Dietetic Association. These association members of Sector Committee 9.5 participate in the investigation, planning, scheduling and implementation of metric conversion in their own specific and related sectors. They also assist in informing and educating the general public, and in particular, housewives.
2.	As representatives of housewives and consumers, the Canadian Home Economics Association and the Consumers' Association of Canada have participated in the development of the metric standards for kitchen measures on which new recipes are now being based. They also contribute to the preparation of information and in the defining of guidelines for housewives as metric conversion is being implemented.
3.	Canadian housewives have traditionally measured their cooking ingredients by volume, and Sector Committee 9.5 of the Metric Commission has recommended a metric standard of 250 ml to replace the 237 ml(8 U.S. fluid ounce) measuring cup used throughout Canada. This is an increase in the size of the measure of only 5 percent and in most cases will allow either old or new recipes to be used interchangeably. So long as housewives keep their present measuring equipment, they can continue to use existing recipes and it is anticipated dual reading equipment will be available in the future.
4.	Since metric conversion, well under way in some sectors, will proceed over a number of years, in others, in ways to be determined by the needs and opportunities in different sectors of the economy, the cost of conversion is, by that fact, undeterminable at this time. Its magnitude will depend on the pace and the phasing of conversion adopted within and without the respective sectors.
5.	In the United States, Congressional Committee hearings scheduled for April 29 and 30 and May 1, 6, 7 and 8, will deal with the passage of metric conversion legislation in the United States Congress. Industry, coordinated by the American National Metric Council, has for about two years been proceeding with metric conversion. Many multi-national corporations in the United States are converting. An amendment to the United States Education Act has been passed by Congress to promote the use of the metric system in educational agencies and institutions. Mexico has used the metric system since 1862.
Order Paper Questions
6.	Experience abroad, particularly in South Africa, New Zealand and Australia, indicates that a well planned, speedy metric conversion supported by timely amendments to legislation will create an environment conducive to a minimum on inconvenience to the general public and economic sectors.
7.	In the White Paper on Metric Conversion in Canada of January 1970, representative national organizations put their views on metric matters before the Government and suggested courses of action ranging from initiation of studies to immediate adoption. Subsequently, all the national representative organizations were requested to respond to a survey prepared by the Metric Commission. These organizations participate directly in the planning, scheduling and implementation of metric conversion in Canada through the committee structure of the Metric Commission.
8.	The White Paper on Metric Conversion of 1970, setting out the policy of the Government and the background for its decision, was placed before Parliament and received unanimous endorsement. The program of guideline dates for metric conversion has the unanimous support of all provinces and of all sectors of the Canadian economy represented on the Steering Committees of the Metric Commission. The adoption of a resolution, approving the program of guideline dates, was introduced by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, on March 17, 1975.
9.	Canada wants to make the change in a manner that will produce the greatest net benefit to the Canadian economy.
10.	(a) The governments of provinces are responsible for metric conversion in the educational system, (b) At a meeting on March 20, 1974, an agreed method of liaison was established between the Metric Commission and the Provincial Departments of Education through the Council of Ministers of Education. Associations related to elementary and secondary, post-secondary non-university, and university and college education are all represented on sector committees within the committee structure of the Metric Commission. The representative committee members of the respective groups and the provincial governments carry out investigation, planning and scheduling towards metric conversion in the educational system. The actual implementation phase is being carried out as described in (a) above, (c) Each provincial government has jurisdiction over its own education conversion plans, and the locations where action is being taken, (d) Not available.

subtopic: TWO-PRICE WHEAT ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR PAYMENTS FOR WHEAT PRODUCED AND SOLD IN CANADA FOR HUMAN CONSUMPTION

speechtext: The House resumed, from Tuesday, May 6, consideration of Bill C-19, to provide for payments in respect of wheat produced and sold in Canada for human consumption in Canada, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Agriculture; and motion No. 1 (Mr. Horner).

subtopic: TWO-PRICE WHEAT ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR PAYMENTS FOR WHEAT PRODUCED AND SOLD IN CANADA FOR HUMAN CONSUMPTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to continue the debate on the amendment, I think first of all I should make the House fully aware that Bill C-19 is a bill to allow Canadian millers to buy wheat at $3.25 a bushel while the government subsidizes the consumer to the tune of $1.75, making the total price received $5. When wheat sells at above $5 a bushel-as the Canadian Wheat Board is pricing wheat now, or at other times above $5 or $6-the farmer, in essence, subsidizes the consumer. My amendment suggests that it might be all right today, but the bill really establishes an agreement that would be in effect for a period of seven years from 1974 to 1980.
My amendment suggests that while it may be all right today, with the cost of production accelerating at the rate it is, we should not lock the farmers into this agreement any longer than 1977, because with inflation and the cost of production rising the farmers may find themselves subsidizing the Canadian consumers more than they can afford. I stated that the Federation of Agriculture certainly agreed that there should be some indexing built into the guaranteed price. They say that if this bill were effective in 1974, and if one took the average increase in the cost of production of 14 per cent last year according to Statistics Canada, the base price should not be $3.25 but $3.67. The Palliser Wheat Growers' Association appeared before the committee. At page 5 of committee report No. 10, Mr. Nelson had this to say:
We discussed it at a directors' meeting two weeks ago and I will tell you what the representative of the wheat growers came up with, a $4.25 floor. We will take a $5 ceiling knowing that we are taking 80 cents, 90 cents to $1 less than the world price-
So, the farmers are fully aware how much they are asked to subsidize the consumers in this issue. The point is that all the farmers are not particularly satisfied with the concept of no indexing in this bill. Mr. Nelson goes on to say at the same page, in reply to a question put to him by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil):
Wheat Payments
That is right. You cannot really rationalize what is going on and what has taken place in the past 12 or 18 months. It would not be inconceivable that we could go to $10 a bushel before spring or in the next two or three years.
They can hardly determine what the price of wheat will be, but every farm group that appeared before the committee wanted the indexing. Mr. Atkinson, of the National Farmers' Union, had this to say:
I think it is rather dangerous to establish policy for seven years on any matter, given current economic conditions. I think it would be most unsatisfactory and it would be more desirable to approach it, at first, from a more enlightened point of view. The seven-year period could be handled if they had an adequate indexing system.
In committee we attempted to index the price of wheat, but that was ruled out of order. We all know that members of the opposition cannot increase government expenditures, so we could not move an amendment to that effect. The best amendments I could come up were the two I filed. We cannot index unless we bind the farmers to a very limited period. In my amendment, the period would be three years which is longer than the period in any agreement signed by workers; at the very most, their agreements run for two years and sometimes 30 months, but rarely for three years.
In what I believe is a reasonable amendment I am suggesting a three-year period from 1974 to 1977, rather than a seven-year period. To give the committee some idea of the situation, I should mention that a similar piece of legislation is now before the Senate of the United States. In the farm prices bill in the United States the Senate has set a floor price for wheat of $3.41. Therefore, it is not out of line to suggest that if we cannot have indexing we should certainly shorten the period concerned, for the benefit of the farmers in this period of rising costs of production.
I think it only fair to point out that the interesting thing about the price of wheat to the miller is that it has not controlled the rise in the price of bread to the consumer. It has not accomplished what was intended. I believe a very comparable study would indicate that in recent years the price of wheat in the United States dropped 30 cents, but the price of bread in the United States increased 15 cents. While we have had a drop in the price of wheat to the Canadian miller, the price of bread has continued to go up in two or three stages. I am not asking for any great changes in the legislation.
If the government's guarantee is any good, if the price of $3.25 is a guarantee to the millers and there is a guaranteed subsidy of $1.75, why should we sign up the farmer for a period of seven years? There could be reinstatement for another three years after 1977 if the costs of production should not go up. There is no need to lock the farmers in for such a long period. In fact, if I were looking at it from a strictly political point of view, I would think the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Lang) is making a grave political error in attempting to treat the farmers so callously by locking them into a period which is longer than the period involved in any collective bargaining agreement today, or even in attempting to negotiate this agreement for a period of anything approaching seven years.
Once again the minister is treating the farmers with a callous disrespect for their intelligence and well-being. In

May 7, 1975
Wheat Payments
this amendment I am offering a logical "out" for the minister. If he accepted the amendment he might gain some respect from the farming community. Personally, I would like to think that he would accept this amendment. I do not think that everyone in the House of Commons should be so political that good ideas which originate on this side cannot be accepted by the other side. I believe that the minister should accept suggestions which are put forward from this side from time to time.
Sometimes government members suggest that we criticize but never offer suggestions or solutions. From time to time the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) asks a member of the opposition, "What is your solution? What would you do?" Now I am putting forward what I would do. I would limit the time period during which this act will be in effect from 1974 until 1977. I think it would be a major improvement because this legislation does not take into consideration the cost of production. If it did, I suppose it could be, in effect, in perpetuity; but since it does not take the cost of production into account, the life of the legislation should be limited so that we could reappraise the situation in 1977, at which time we could adjust the floor price.
Members of the committee have suggested from time to time that the minister would automatically adjust the floor price when he found it justifiable to do so. But there was no doubt about the minister's view on this subject; he left no doubt that the ceiling will not be adjusted and that it will remain set.
With regard to the over-all wheat situation, hon. members might have noticed a story in yesterday's newspapers which stated that the prospects for a bumper crop of winter wheat in the United States are good, but that stocks on hand in the five major exporting countries are 300 million tons less than last year. So it appears that prices will remain relatively high. Of course, when one starts to price wheat internationally, one finds that much depends on the U.S.S.R. and China and that it is very difficult to gauge exactly what prices will be before one knows the intentions of those two countries. In any case, it appears that prices will remain high this year and possibly next year, and if that is so farmers will continue to subsidize the Canadian consumer.
With regard to prices remaining high, I should like to quote Mr. Vogel, chairman of the Canadian Wheat Board who was before the Standing Committee on Agriculture on November 14. As recorded at page 15 of committee proceedings No. 7, Mr. Vogel said:
It would then take probably one year at least to replenish supplies to a point where most people in the world would feel comfortable, which tends to say that prices would remain relatively firm even next year, even though perhaps not as high as they are now. That would take us until at least 1976, maybe even 1977. To the 1980s, though, you would be really crystal-balling.
I say that the amendment which would limit the life of the bill until 1977, at which time we would be better able to gauge whether we want to tie farmers down to this floor price and to the ceiling of $5 a bushel on wheat consumed in Canada, should be adopted. The Wheat Board price, it seems to me, is still $5 a bushel although the

international price is below that. To be exact, the asking price for Canadian wheat is still $5.16.

speechtext:
That is interesting, because the Wheat Board had an offer recently of less than $5 and they might have taken it. Certainly the price of wheat has come down on the international market to about $2 a bushel. But never mind what the price of wheat will be; we all know that costs are going up considerably so long as this government has no control over inflation. That is where the problem lies. We believe that rather than accept a fixed floor price of $3.25, we should be able to pass on additional costs to the Canadian bakers and consumers. Everyone else is passing on their costs, so why should not the agricultural industry do the same?
I really believe that the price of wheat does not greatly affect the price of a loaf of bread; it is only about a 3 per cent factor in the price of a loaf of bread. Most of the cost is in other ingredients and in the labour that goes into baking the bread. It is demonstrated in an American study that the price of wheat on the U.S. market has dropped 30 per cent from a year ago, but the price of a loaf of bread is up 15 per cent. We have had a similar increase in Canada. I believe that limiting the price of wheat until 1980 would not really keep down the price of bread to the Canadian consumer; bread prices will continue to rise. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) can make all the noise he wants, but sometimes an inflationary economy justifies an increase in the price of bread.
So I urge the Minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board not to be so political in his actions, to look at some of the ideas put forward by members on this side of the House, and to accept what I am certain most members of the opposition parties agree is a very good suggestion which will improve the bill before us in the interests of farmers caught in a price squeeze.

subtopic: TWO-PRICE WHEAT ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR PAYMENTS FOR WHEAT PRODUCED AND SOLD IN CANADA FOR HUMAN CONSUMPTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with a great deal of pleasure that I second the motion now before us, because if you look at the two motions under consideration you will see that the amendments moved to this bill by the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) cover the basic objections of this party to the legislation.
Quite frankly, I am somewhat disturbed by the attitude of the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Lang), of stubbornly refusing to incorporate an indexing system to reflect the increase in the cost of production, a system which has been applied in many other programs of the government, such as agricultural programs, pension programs and others. Pension programs, of course, take into consideration the increase in the cost of living. I want to make it abundantly clear that we as a party have always supported the principle of a two-price system for wheat, but in saying that I emphasize that it must be a two-price system that is adequate and will accurately reflect the increase in the cost of production. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has always argued this rather forcefully and we agree with that position. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) indicated in a recent communique that the prices which farmers are getting now are somewhat below the cost of production.
May 7, 1975

This fact should be recognized. But what have we here? We have nothing more than a bill which amounts to a seven-year freeze. We oppose that concept.
I sincerely think that the minister should recognize the fact that if he were to incorporate an indexing provision, or if he were, so to speak, to shorten the contract which would provide an opportunity for reviewing the pricing structure, this bill would be accepted not only by parliament but by the producers of Canada. I am sure that was the major objective in drafting the bill. As the hon. member for Crowfoot pointed out, surely no union involved in the collective bargaining process would accept a proposition such as this. The incomes of most people are based upon anticipated or projected costs of living. Most manufacturing firms base the cost of their products on anticipated cost of production. But here we have a situation where the cost of production factor is not taken into consideration and no adjustment is allowed for: there is a seven-year fixed price.
We had similar objections to the grain stabilization bill, which we have just concluded. But it, in effect, averages farmers' incomes on the previous five years, so surely it is time we became a little more forward-looking in our approach to agriculture, particularly in the grains industry. It is time we dealt with it in such a way that we can effectively and realistically consider those elements which go toward the production of that commodity.
The minister's position on this bill is inconsistent with stated government policy. As the hon. member for Crowfoot pointed out, in the absence of an over-all anti-inflationary policy or pricing and incomes policy, the government has embarked upon a program of indexing to protect the purchasing power of Canadians in reflecting the cost of living and, indeed, in areas of production in agriculture to reflect the increases in the cost of production. It has been stated that many elements of inflation are beyond the control of this government. I believe that a great deal of the inflationary pressures are domestically created and that effective measures could be introduced. Failing that, the government has undertaken to ameliorate or to try to cushion the effects of inflation, so we have the program of indexing.
It is rather amusing to note that that is the nature of the stabilization bill the Minister of Agriculture recently introduced: it took into consideration the cost of production. In other words, guaranteed floor prices would be adjusted to reflect changes in production costs. That is an agricultural bill and it was proposed by this government. The beef stabilization plan is another program in which provision is made to index production costs. A whole host of similar measures have been brought forward by this government. They take into consideration provisions for increases in the cost of production, and it seems to me it is rather unrealistic on the part of this minister to deviate from that stated government policy. It is difficult for me to understand, and it seems that by acceptance of either one of these amendments, if the minister refuses to incorporate an indexing system, parliament or the government will have an opportunity to review this seven-year contract and adjust it as may be necessary.
Wheat Payments
We all know that input costs are generally increasing. The Edmonton Journal of January 20, 1975, reporting on the agricultural outlook conference, said the following:
The Canadian farmer is being warned to brace himself for a year of reduced profits from the fruits of his labour.
Federal agriculture officials predict another large increase in farm operating expenses will wipe out a slight rise in revenues in 1975 ...
Last year, gross farm income climbed nearly 26 per cent to $9.2 billion, according to preliminary Statistics Canada figures. But a $1 billion jump in operating costs meant net farm income increased only $50 million, to $3.39 billion.
It seems absolutely ludicrous for this government to disregard this important element in a so-called effective two-price wheat system. We are talking about the increase in production costs over a period of seven years. I have before me a table which outlines the increase in production costs, a five-year record of list prices and 1975 projections in respect of key inputs, dated May 1, in central Saskatchewan. These are largely inputs which go toward the production of grain. It is an article printed in the Free Press Weekly Report on Farming of November 16, 1974, and it cites the tremendous increase in basic commodity inputs which have been registered over a five-year period. For example, 11-48-0 fertilizer, 50-pound bags, per ton in 1970 cost $103; in 1975, the projected price is $200. The price of 128-ounce 2-4-D Ester, per five-gallon pail, in 1970 was $24.95; in 1975, $70. Carbyne, in 1970, cost $59.90; in 1975, $75. I could go on with grain bins, baler twine, diesel tractors, combines and diesel fuel: all these items have increased tremendously over a five-year period.
We need only consider the tragic change which occurred in the last year. For example, the farm input index from 1972 to 1973 rose 19 per cent, and the 1974 index rose by 15 per cent. Surely, with that type of historical pattern, it is only natural, if this government believes in stabilization and in producing a reasonable income for prairie wheat farmers, particularly when we consider the domestic price, that some means should be found to compensate and adjust for realistic input costs. Failing that, the bill does not really get to the principle and the heart of the subject.
It seems that there are many arguments for acceptance of these two amendments. I am sure the hon. member for Crowfoot would have no objection to acceptance of either one, because I think the principle embodied in both of them meets our major objection to this legislation. Quite frankly, I do not think this bill is worth the paper it is written on unless one of the amendments is accepted. I see no reason why the government should not accept one or the other, because the bill as it stands is a complete contradiction of and total deviation from stated government policy.
All I can say is that if the government and the minister in charge of the Wheat Board, who is the person who has to pilot this bill through the House, fail to recognize this inherent deficiency, that will reflect the intransigent attitude of the minister. We have a Minister of Agriculture who accepts indexing, and we have a minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board who does not accept indexing. Mr. Speaker, I say there is a glaring deviation and a glaring inconsistency in the views of the cabinet and the government. All the farm organizations support the two-price system. The 1975 policy statement of the western agricultural conference recommended at page 5:

Wheat Payments
An adequate two-price system for all grains used for domestic human and industrial consumption, including grain used for distilling, brewing and malting, miscellaneous chemicals, explosives, etc.
That the Government of Canada amend the current price arrangement with the Canadian Wheat Board respecting wheat for domestic human consumption, which would provide for an annual review of the guaranteed floor price, so that the floor would reflect changes in the index of farm input costs.
That sums up the situation quite well, Mr. Speaker. A press release issued before the minister in charge of the Wheat Board headed west to talk about transportation boasted about the importance of communicating with the farm community and quoted the minister as follows:
During my 5!d years as minister responsible for the federal government's programs and policies affecting the western grain industry, I have found these encounters with producers to be both informative and productive. I am looking forward to this next week in the same light.
Surely, if that dialogue is to be meaningful, the minister should pay attention to the wishes of the body of agriculture represented by the major farm organizations such as the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and the National Farmers' Union. In this regard, the minister should immediately consider one or both of the amendments. It is interesting to notice that there is a degree of consultation taking place at the moment on the government benches, Mr. Speaker. Maybe the hon. member for Battleford-Kin-dersley (Mr. Mclsaac) and the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale) can pool their wisdom for the minister and help him see the light.
I hope the minister will stand in his place and at least recognize the deficiency in this bill which has been echoed by members in this House and in committee. If he has the interest of the grain producers at heart, surely he will see fit to accept the amendments proposed by the hon. member for Crowfoot.

Mr. Speaker, this issue, as well as the one arising under the subsequent amendment, was thoroughly discussed in committee. It seems to show that hon. members opposite are in some doubt about where they stand on such things as guarantees and long-term agreements for the sale of grain. I would remind hon. members that, as I made clear in committee, the question of how long the agreement or price relationship between the Canadian Wheat Board and the domestic market should be was put to the Wheat Board before it was adopted in the present form by the government.
As the body which can ordinarily enter into long-term and short-term contracts for farmers, the Canadian Wheat Board was asked if, with a price range lower than the one before us now, they would prefer an agreement for five, or seven, years. They opted for the seven-year period because of what they saw as a protection in the floor price of $3.25. The Canadian Wheat Board confirmed this at the time of its appearance before the chief commissioner. It is essentially the business of the Canadian Wheat Board to enter into contracts like this.
The principle of long-term contracts and international wheat agreements is one which is ordinarily applauded by hon. members opposite. Certainly, it is consistently

applauded by members of the New Democratic Party and in the rather more traditional way it is applauded and not applauded by the more inconsistent members of the Conservative Party who always seem to be on all sides of any issue.
The other day the agriculture critic of the Conservative Party, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) came down emphatically in favour of long-term agreements, international agreements, firm agreements. Obviously, in those circumstances we have to make some judgment about price. There has to be a price range with that kind of agreement that will balance the forces at work. We cannot expect a price range where the minimum is somewhere near the maximum of history. What we have here is a very good arrangement. This is the first time that the price of wheat in Canada has moved above $3 except for the very special circumstances of one wartime occasion. For the first time in history, the price has moved rapidly above $3 and we have a seven-year agreement with the price in the range of $3.25 to $5 in terms of the return to the producer. Surely that is to the advantage of producers. The Canadian Wheat Board saw that advantage.
The Saskatchewan Wheat Pool over the years has consistently favoured international agreements and recognizes their value. That is why, in a statement of policy which followed their last meeting, they indicated support for international wheat arrangements with firm prices. On page 8 of the statement they indicated that they liked having the principle applied here and that they liked the idea of an annual review. In fact, an annual review was included in this legislation in the course of committee hearings.
Hon. members opposite like to take the view that ministers, perhaps myself in particular, are inflexible. I may be inflexible when dealing with certain of the very political pressures and doctrines of the parties opposite when they are as inconsistent as members of the official opposition, but my record shows flexibility in response to reasoned arguments, particularly those from farmers and farm organizations.
In this particular case I could have said that an agreement for seven years of $3.25 to $5 looked very good in September, 1973, and that price should be binding over the whole seven-year period. I could reasonably have taken that position. If the Wheat Board had entered into a similar agreement with the principal buyers in other countries, it is likely that nothing more than that would be said about the prices within the agreement. Both would want to be bound by the floor and the ceiling and not move away from them.
But I recognize the concern of farmers that suddenly certain prices in this country have begun to rise more rapidly than was contemplated at the time of the 1973 decision to go to a $3.25 and $5 range, even though the $3.25 figure was 25 cents higher than had previously been both the maximum and minimum and was in itself a record price, and the $5 was something that until a few months before had never been dreamed of by anyone outside of the Canadian Wheat Board and those who shared their knowledge of international circumstances.
May 7, 1975

The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale) put the proposition to the committee that an annual review might be desirable because of what has happened in terms of prices, and that we should be looking at the annual cost of production and the returns in total coming to farmers. That change is now found as clause 5(3) in the bill as it emerged from committee. That is the answer to both the first amendment and the second amendment of the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner), Mr. Speaker.
I should add that in the course of the committee deliberations one hon. member saw fit to make sure that the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Assiniboia was distributed to farm organizations. The response from them was extremely good and generally approved of the amendment. The resolution from the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool used the same words almost exactly. They said that the agreement between the government and the Canadian Wheat Board should be amended to provide for an annual review of the guaranteed floor price and subsidy limits so that the floor and ceiling would level changes in producer costs. In other words, the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool endorsed the amendment proposed in committee in answer to representations from farm organizations and the reasonable arguments that the hon. member for Assiniboia put before the committee at that time.
May I say one further word about price. Hon. members opposite blow hot and cold on the question of price. After saying that prices will never be as high as this again, they quickly say that we are facing disaster, that prices will go through every floor known and we shall be in deep trouble. Once again they take both sides of an issue. The fact is that prices have generally been within the range of the agreement. The end returns for the Canadian Wheat Board pool for the year ending in 1974, which really means the selling period to October, 1974, were well under $5. This represents the final value of wheat sold through the Canadian Wheat Board.
During that period, although prices reached some of their highest peaks, the returns when they were in represented less than $5; therefore the farmer was getting from the treasury full benefit bearing in mind the international price. The price since has weakened. I hope prices will go higher again. The fact is that this agreement was struck at a time when it looked to the Wheat Board, the best protector of the farmer, as reasonable in price terms in relation to the international market. They saw the value of a seven-year agreement as opposed to one of three years or five years when the choice was open to them. It seems to me that that ought, for all hon. members, including Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition, to conclude the matter in favour of the bill as it now stands.
Surely we want to keep this guarantee for the seven-year period. I hope, therefore, all hon. members will join in opposing the amendment. It may be that the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) on reflection will want to withdraw it, and I am sure members of the House would accommodate him in that regard.

subtopic: TWO-PRICE WHEAT ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR PAYMENTS FOR WHEAT PRODUCED AND SOLD IN CANADA FOR HUMAN CONSUMPTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to participate in this debate and support the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Homer).
Wheat Payments
Disaster occasionally strikes western Canadians. The greatest disaster that has struck them is the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang). In no way has the minister been flexible or shown that he intends to listen to reason or appreciates the difficulties of western farmers. Not long ago we saw the upper hierarchy of the Liberal Party called to Calgary to attend the western economic opportunities conference. People were wondering what had come over the Liberal Party. The Liberals wondered why western Canadians were complaining. Well, we were complaining about the situation which has existed for some time. The minister's present position is one more ground for complaint.
The minister tried to suggest, a few minutes ago, that we are not in favour of long-term agreements. We are. But can the minister point to any other agreement which is to stand for seven years? Why are other agreements for a shorter period? Why does he want to pin farmers down to a price which is to stand for seven years? The government is in favour of long-term agreements. However, we do not know where we stand; there is no floor and no ceiling price and we do not know what we can look forward to.
The minister takes the position that the western farmer is to be held down to a certain price for seven years. How can the minister justify his position? Who can say if $5 will be sufficient two years from now, let alone seven? We are only asking for this matter to be reconsidered two years from now. The provisions of the bill can again be implemented then. There is no suggestion they would change. We are merely asking for the opportunity to review the situation in two years. Let parliament approve this measure again at that time. After all, the composition of the House of Commons in 1977, barring any unforeseen elections which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) may call, will be the same as at present. This parliament will still be in existence and hon. members opposite will still have the power to push through any legislation they want. We are merely asking the government for the sort of consideration we wanted when we debated the grain stabilization bill.
Western Canadians do not trust this minister. For years we asked for a two-price system; we were not given consideration except during the period when the Conservatives were in office, led by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). That is when we were given acreage payments in lieu of a two-price system. In those days the dollar was worth a dollar. In those days a budget of less than $6 billion was enough for all federal expenditures, including health, defence, and so on. Today the government spends more than $30 billion-and it has come along with a niggardly 25 cents for farmers. Where is the breakthrough?
The cost of machinery in the last year rose by 38 per cent, yet the minister wants to tie every farmer down to a price for seven years, until 1980. I know farm organizations have made representations, I know there has been agitation for a two-price system, and I know that someone could push the argument to the point where the minister will simply refuse to move. Nevertheless, a lot of people are in favour of that principle.
No responsible farm leader will say honestly that he wants prices held at $5 until 1980. How then, can this

May 7, 1975
Wheat Payments
minister make that suggestion? Further, how can he suggest that reconsideration of this measure in two or three years will in any way jeopardize or change the measure? We bring the Canadian Wheat Board Act before the House from time to time; there is nothing permanent about it. Why cannot we do the same with this bill? After all, it breaks no new ground: why should we be stuck with seven years? It will be seven years bad luck so far as some people are concerned. They know inflation is not being dealt with and they know that costs are rising sharply.
An agricultural conference several months ago pointed out that farmers' incomes would drop by 15 per cent. We know they will drop, but we know prices are going up. Fertilizer costs have already tripled, and machinery costs have gone up by 38 per cent. Inflation has hit the farmer from every angle. Why, then, should we pin ourselves down for seven years? I cannot see what the minister is afraid of. Is he afraid the consumer will be unreasonable? The consumer is going to be reasonable. This minister and this government do not seem to understand that the farmer is the biggest consumer in Canada. These farmers specialize. They do not have their farms cluttered with every product they require; they produce one product and get everything else they require at the market. They no longer tan their hides. As a matter of fact, they buy their milk, butter and eggs. They are consumers. It is not as though the farmers were arguing against the consumers; they are consumers.
The minute there is buoyancy in the economy as far as the farmer is concerned, everyone benefits. Manufacturers benefit. When the farmers think there is a possibility of getting a payment, they spend that money in advance. They know what has happened with the price of machinery, for example. Long before they even receive the money, they make arrangements at the bank to borrow the maximum amount they can. Because of the great demand for borrowing, parliament recognized that fact and increased the amount it is possible to borrow. Everyone knows prices have gone up because we increased the amount that farmers can borrow.
We are simply asking the government not to tie the hands of the farmers for seven years. We plead with the minister to be reasonable and not to be so entrenched in his ways. Because the idea comes from a member of the official opposition, it is immediately discarded. Surely it must mean something to the minister that Liberals have been defeated time and again in western Canada. The reason is obvious. The minister has his eyes and ears closed with regard to western farmers. For all his forays into western Canada, the Prime Minister will not help the situation unless the minister shows a willingness to recognize the plight of these people.
As was pointed out by the hon. member for Crowfoot, we in this party cannot introduce a motion to ask for more money: that is not the right of members of the opposition. The minister has that right; however, he ties it down to a fixed price. Instead of waiting until 1982, we simply ask the minister to reconsider this question a few years from now. There is nothing on the horizon to indicate that costs will go down. There is a possibility that the price of grain will go down. If the minister does not want to recognize

the principle of indexing, perhaps we could come to him at that time and ask him to reconsider his position. As a matter of fact, it might work out very handily; by that time we might be ready for another election. The minister could bring forward an amendment and increase the price even if only on a one-year basis. He could tell the farmers of western Canada that he was increasing the price even though it may not be below the $5. He could say he was increasing the price because of the increased cost of production, inflationary trends and so on.
The amount involved would not be terribly great. It would involve the consumption of 50 million or 60 million bushels of wheat. Even if he increased the price at that time by $1, considering the way this government blows money left, right and centre, $50 million or $60 million in another two or three years would not break the back of this government. After all, they have been very wasteful. Maybe by that time we could cut down some of the expenses of the Prime Minister's office.
One would think we were asking for the moon. However, we are only asking for the same principle that applies to every labour organization and pensioner. We do not want to be tied down to a seven-year period. We want an even break. What we are asking for is not unreasonable. We want what every other segment of the economy is getting. If we do not get a better price, we want consideration within a few years. We do not want the minister to shelve this problem for seven years, which is exactly what he wants to do.
Because they want the principle of a two-price system, the members of the New Democratic Party voted against this suggestion in committee. However, on reflection I am sure they will realize that what we are asking for is very reasonable. I think they, too, would like to have this question reconsidered. I feel they will even support us at this time because they have found out the farmers want to be like other Canadians. Despite the comments the minister has made, if he would reverse his position and be on the side of the farmer, it would not be anything to be ashamed of, but it would be a credit to him.

subtopic: TWO-PRICE WHEAT ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR PAYMENTS FOR WHEAT PRODUCED AND SOLD IN CANADA FOR HUMAN CONSUMPTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say that on the motion I am of two minds. As I said on second reading, our party fully supports a two-price system in Canada: one price for grain used domestically for human consumption, with support from the federal treasury to, in effect, subsidize the consumer, and the farmer getting a reasonable price for his grain. Since the government has finally come around to agreeing to the principle of a two-price system for wheat, I repeat the question: Why just wheat? In all the years we have made this proposal, we have said grain. If it is logical for wheat, it is logical that it should be applied to all grains for whatever period of time is provided in the legislation. Oats, barley, rye, flax and rapeseed sold in Canada for human consumption should also be eligible for a two-price system.
It is a habit of this government and the Liberal Party in general that whenever they finally come around to a good principle, they only go part way or, at best, halfway. There is continual battling to get them to move further than they normally do. I understand the fears of the hon. member who moved this amendment and those of the other speak-
May 7, 1975

ers from the Conservative Party. If I had more confidence in getting some fast results from this minister in terms of adjusting prices to reflect increased costs of production, I would have little worry about the length of the term in this legislation. I appreciate that the hon. member who moved the amendment also does not have that confidence. The government did at least move slightly to amend the bill so as to provide for an annual review, but it is still too softly worded, I think. The bill says that the minister "shall review", but then it goes on to say "with a view to recommending to the governor in council changes in the price system which would reflect the cost of production". I would rather it said "and shall recommend to the governor in council changes which would reflect the cost of production". One could then agree that the amendment would be totally unnecessary.
I am still inclined not to agree with motion No. 1. The seven-year guarantee at a minimum of $3.25 was a success in finally getting the minister to take such a step, after repeated demands from prairie farmers and farm organizations over many years. Having got that much out of him, I am somewhat reluctant to lessen the length of time. I fear that if we reduce the period from 1980 to 1977 as proposed in the motion, this would leave the door wide open, if we are still stuck with this minister in charge of the Wheat Board in 1977, for him not to further extend the two-price system. He might do less than is already provided in the bill.
This is why I am inclined to vote against the motion. We run the risk of the matter being left wide open in 1977 and of losing even what we have in this measure, especially if we then happen to be in a period of recession and the Minister of Finance is still screaming for restraint and trying to cut back on all the different departments of government. I wonder whether the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) has thought of the risk. Whatever inadequacies there are in the legislation, I think shortening of the length of time, on the other side of the coin, does constitute a risk.
With regard to calculating the cost of production, the minister and the majority of the committee refused to accept an amendment which both the Conservatives and my own party members proposed regarding a cost of production escalator. They refused it on the excuse that it would be very difficult to arrive at a proper calculation of the cost of production. I understand that the Department of National Revenue, under the Income Tax Act, has no problem arriving at the cost of production of a farmer because it is what the department allows him for his costs. I am sure that even a computer analysis of farm costs shown on the income tax returns of the grain farmers of western Canada would produce a pretty good figure, because you can be sure that the farmers attach every bill of expense they can so as to reduce their income tax liability.
Statistics Canada has done a lot of work in this field. There have been several farm management studies, and farm management groups in Canada have carried out extensive work on the question. I believe that two or three of the universities in the prairie provinces have done work on the matter. All these sources can be used in arriving
Wheat Payments
very quickly at a cost of production calculation that will at least reflect an average cost of production in Canadian Wheat Board areas.
I asked the minister in committee, after the amendment calling for mandatory review by the minister on an annual basis was passed, whether he would be good enough to consider carrying out a review of the 1974 experience, and he said he would not. He refused in the committee and said his first annual review would commence after 1975. This means that the farmers have lost an additional year in regard to having their cost of production taken into account and reflected in the prices to be paid under this legislation.
I should like to hear the minister assure the House that he has had a slight change of heart for the better; that he will in fact make a review, under the legislation, of the 1974 experience and that he will make appropriate recommendations to the governor in council this fall, or as soon as he possibly can, regarding additional funds. I do not think there can be any question that the increased cost of production in 1974 will be, if not the highest then certainly one of the highest for some years ahead. All of us know about the kind of jump in farm costs that occurred in 1974, particularly for products related in any way to oil, such as farm fuels, fertilizers, farm machinery and farm machinery parts. Then, of course, interest rates increased. I submit that farm costs made the highest jump in history during the year 1974, yet the minister does not want to make a review of that year.
The legislation provides that the minister shall review on an annual basis. The amendment does not ask that he shall review, commencing in 1975; it just says he shall review on an annual basis. We have had the 1974 experience. Although I am no lawyer, I interpret the amendment moved by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale) which the committee accepted to mean that the minister must begin now to make an annual review of the cost of production in 1974. I trust that his officials would draw on Statistics Canada, the Department of National Revenue and any other source necessary in order to come up with a good calculation of the average increase in cost of production.
I appreciate that this cannot be done farm by farm, that cost of production varies from one part of a designated area to another. But surely the total increase in costs can be arrived at. This will take several weeks of work and statistical study, and I hope the minister is already working on the matter. If he is not, then it seems to me the minister should be-at least as I interpret the legislation. I, for one, will want a legal opinion on the question; I am not just going to rely on the opinion of the Minister of Justice. It seems to me from the way the amendment reads, and the way the legislation as amended reads, that the minister must carry out a review for last year. If he were to do so, I would be even more inclined to vote against motion No. 1, because such action would at least restore a little confidence that until 1980 farmers would get a fair shake in terms of any increase in the cost of production since it would be reflected in the price they receive for hard wheat and durum.
The other point I want to make is this. The minister failed to respond to suggestions that he do something

Wheat Payments
about how durum wheat should be treated in the legislation. When one looks quickly at the bill, one gets the impression that the floor for durum is $5.75, whereas it is in fact $3.25. As and when the world price drops for durum wheat below the $5.75 figure, so does the floor in this bill drop, and it keeps dropping until it gets down to $3.25.
I submit, as many farmers have, that historically durum has always brought a somewhat better price than hard wheat. I appreciate that you cannot maintain a $2 or $3 per bushel spread between hard wheat and durum because you would then be up to your eyeballs in durum and would not have enough hard wheat. Farmers would, quite naturally, grow more durum than we could use or sell. It is fair that at least a 50-cent or even a $1 differential should be maintained between the price of durum and hard wheat. I still think that should be the case. I hope the minister will agree to amending his own legislation, although it is a little late to do that at this point in time. When he makes his annual review and appropriate recommendations to the governor in council, he could bring in additional amendments to the legislation to accomplish that very thing regarding the price of durum wheat.
The whole principle of long-term guarantees and contracts for farmers has been fought for by my party and farm organizations for many years. We have finally obtained a commitment from this government in respect of at least $3.25 per bushel. That is insufficient in my opinion since it only applies to wheat and does not do a proper job in accounting for increased costs of production, but at least it is a beginning. The fact that we have finally succeeded in getting something in this legislation that gives the farmer the assurance of some certainty in respect of what he is going to get for several years causes me to object to the motion. I object to it, as well, because I am fearful that if we shorten the time to 1977 from 1980, the whole thing will be left wide open and we run the grave risk of losing what we have in this legislation, getting less or not getting anything better for the years after 1977. On balance, I have to oppose the motion.
One can hope that the annual review will produce some results and I hope that the confidence of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale) is not misplaced in that regard. I hope the hon. member will add his support to my suggestion that the first review should be carried out for 1974. It is very likely that the cost of production in 1975 will not increase as much as it did in 1974, so the farmers would lose out in respect of the worst year in relation to rising costs of production. I hope the hon. member will attempt to persuade the minister to make that review on a retroactive basis for the crop year that has just finished.

subtopic: TWO-PRICE WHEAT ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR PAYMENTS FOR WHEAT PRODUCED AND SOLD IN CANADA FOR HUMAN CONSUMPTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have only a few points to make on the bill as I do not want to repeat what has just been said. I support the amendment. I am sure the wheat farmers in western Canada would be satisfied to have either of the suggested principles included in this bill. I think it is necessary to make some points in relation to the cost of production, and I intend to put on record some statistics from Statistics Canada which show this dramatic increase.

The proposed amendment of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale) is vague in relation to whether the minister has to bring forward these aspects of production costs. The Conservative Party has been consistent, contrary to what the minister suggests, in having the best interests of the farmers at heart and in attempting to see that the farmers get a proper deal. We are concerned that if the price of wheat increases above $5 a bushel, the farmer will not from now until 1980 be able to take advantage of that price increase in respect of the number of bushels consumed in Canada, but he will still have to absorb the increased cost of production during the years from now until 1980.
I appreciate that this bill ultimately provides a consumer subsidy and the farmers, being consumers, will be able to take advantage of the price of bread remaining relatively stable. One very important element has not been taken into consideration, and that is the increasing cost of producing wheat on the prairies. If production costs increase as they have in the past, the farmer will be penalized in respect of the amount of wheat he sells. Essentially, he will have to make a contribution rather than realizing a slim profit or even breaking even. To set the price per bushel for such a long period without making some concrete provision for escalating input costs is totally unrealistic.
The guaranteed price is basically $3.25 a bushel. Perhaps a year ago, or even today, $3.25 would be a satisfactory price. However, we certainly have no assurance that in 11 years $3.25 or, for that matter, even $5 will be sufficient to cover the increase in input expenditures. The Federation of Agriculture appeared before the committee and stated that since this bill was introduced to the House the cost of production had already risen 14.6 per cent, particularly in western Canada where this grain is produced. Given this fact, the figure of $3.25 should increase to approximately $3.67 a bushel. If the price of wheat should fall below the $3.25 guarantee, the farmer would only receive the same price per bushel regardless of his increased production costs.
We all know how important wheat production is at this time, particularly when the world is finding itself in a deficit food position. We have even heard pleas for increased wheat production here in this House. Surely we must give more consideration to the producers of wheat than is currently being given in Bill C-19. The agricultural sector is the very backbone of our economy, and the grain producers make up a very substantial percentage of this agricultural bloc. Only through a demonstration of fairness and a willingness to consider their arguments can we encourage them to increase their production of No. 1 wheat.
Statistics Canada is today putting out figures on the increased costs of farm production. It would be very easy for the minister to use those statistics as a basis for increasing the $3.25 price. The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) has shown how the costs increased dramatically during 1974. I should like to put on record the percentage increases according to Statistics Canada. Statistics Canada has stated that total farm input costs increased, between 1973 and 1974, by 27.3 per cent based on 1961 dollars. The report has four columns in
May 7, 1975

which they show that the cost of land and farm buildings increased, between 1973 and 1974, by 16.1 per cent. It is well known that farmers must increase their land holdings from time to time and update their old buildings or build new ones.
Farm machinery and motor vehicles have increased by 18.1 per cent, farm labour has increased by 39.4 per cent, and all the other materials used in the production of agricultural products have increased by 39 per cent. This is in the period between 1973 and 1974. To project that from 1974 to 1975, if we look at the industrial price index we see that the cost of production will increase at approximately the same rate as it did during the 1973-74 period. That is why it is so important that either of the amendments of the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) be accepted by the House. The amendment placed before the committee by the hon. member for Assiniboia takes us a short way toward obtaining that principle, but I think far better than that would be an amendment to the bill that would assure the farmer that the increased cost of production in fact would be added to the base price he would receive.
Another point I should like to bring before the House is the fact that, while many people may be pessimistic concerning the price of wheat, a number of witnesses who appeared before the committee said that the price in fact could go very much higher in the next number of years than it is today. We have been accused of blowing hot and cold concerning the price of wheat. That may be so. Perhaps the farmers as they look at the fluctuations in prices and input costs are a little leery of the future. But these witnesses, who I believe are in the know because they deal with the grain situation from day to day, have stated that the price of wheat could go as high as $10 a bushel. I should like to quote from page 5 of the Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence, issue No. 10. The chairman of the Pallis-er Wheat Growers' Association had this to say in reply to a question put to him by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil):
That is right. You cannot really rationalize what is going on and what has taken place in the past 12 or 18 months. It would not be inconceivable that we could go to $10 a bushel before spring or in the next two or three years.
The Washington agricultural outlook conference had the same thing to say: this was also brought before the committee. It was stated in that report that if we can pay the international price in Canada, it is quite conceivable we could reach a price of $10 a bushel in the future. These are the predictions of people who have studied the situation. I believe western wheat farmers are optimistic that the price will increase and that they will be able to meet their cost of production but they are concerned that if in the next two or three years the price should go up they would be committed to a maximum of $5 for their wheat even if the price should go beyond that. If the farmer does not receive a proper return for his product, he may well go into the production of other forms of grain. I think this would be disastrous to our economy because a large portion of our export wealth is based on wheat. It is important that we see that farmers do not go into other types of production because of being locked into an agreement under this bill.
Wheat Payments
I think it is important that we consider these two amendments and pass one or the other in order to make this a better bill for the western wheat growers. I hope the minister and other members will take note of this and will look favourably at the amendments.
