subtopic: TWO-PRICE WHEAT ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR PAYMENTS FOR WHEAT PRODUCED AND SOLD IN CANADA FOR HUMAN CONSUMPTION
speechtext:
That Bill C-19, an act to provide for payments in respect of wheat produced and sold in Canada for human consumption in Canada, be amended at page 3 by (a) deleting the word "and" in line 40 (b) deleting the period at the end of line 44 and substituting therefor ";and" (c) adding immediately after line 44 the following paragraph: "(c) regarding payments authorized under section 4 of a bushel of wheat consumed in Canada: that each year the Canadian Wheat Board, through the minister in charge, report to parliament the average estimated increase in the cost of production.".
He said: Mr. Speaker, there are two significant things about this amendment which I should like to draw to the attention of the House before a decision is reached on it. First of all, the amendment suggests that the Canadian Wheat Board estimate the cost of production. It is not suggested that the minister, for political reasons one way or another, or that some other group should make the estimation, but that the Canadian Wheat Board should estimate the cost of production and the increase in the cost of production each year. Then, through the minister, that figure would be publicly reported in the House of Commons so that everybody would know what in fact was happening concerning the farmer's cost of production in respect of products under this bill which are sold for domestic consumption.
A few minutes ago the minister said that the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale) had moved an

May 7, 1975
Wheat Payments
amendment in committee which he thought would take care of an annual review. That amendment can be found at page 4 of the reprinted bill. It reads:
The minister shall, on an annual basis and in consultation with the producers, review the provisions of this act-
I should like to think that any minister would annually look at the provisions of an act which came under his jurisdiction. I think it would be an insult to a minister to have to be told to do that. I believe it is improper for a minister to be told in a bill that he should do his job. The amendment goes on to say:
-and all related regulations enacted by the governor in council with a view to making such recommendations to the governor in council as are appropriate in the light of prevailing costs of production of wheat and returns to producers.
I have read many wishy-washy words around the House of Commons and have seen some wishy-washy words in pieces of legislation, but from my point of view this amendment to the bill does nothing. It does not enhance the bill. If the minister is doing his job, certainly he would tell his cabinet colleagues about the problems in the part of the agricultural industry for which he is responsible, namely, the wheat farmer and the Canadian Wheat Board. Certainly he would tell the governor in council about the problems of increased costs which the farmers have to put up with.
In looking at committee proceedings No. 12, I find that the hon. member for Assiniboia had quite a lot to say about costs going up or down. At page 12 of the proceedings he is reported to have said the following in reply to Mr. Atkinson of the National Farmers Union who spoke about the squeeze in which farmers would find themselves if a fixed ceiling were set, a squeeze brought about by the escalation in the cost of production:
The legislation is, of course, flexible on that point; it allows that figure to move up and down.
I do not know how much it allows it to move up and down, unless the hon. member is considering adjusting the subsidy that the government puts in at $1.75. If the hon. member wants it lowered to $1.75, then that is a pretty interesting concept. I would hate to think the minister would do that, or that he would pay any attention to his former side-kick in this regard. The hon. member went on to say:
The other issue which is really quite a different one is whether the $5 present talk that is in the legislation is realistic, given the nature of world prices at any particular moment in time. I wonder whether an indexing feature, although it would deal with the base price problem, would really solve any concerns that some people might have about the problem at the other end.
It is interesting to note that every farm organization that has come before the committee, including the Ontario Wheat Farmers, the National Farmers Union and the Pal-liser Wheat Growers, has stated that indexing is necessary. On page 5 of committee proceedings No. 10, Mr. Nelson, former president of the Palliser Wheat Growers' Association, spoke about the escalating factors in the cost of production. He was replying to a question put to him by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) who said:

You mentioned that your executive, in discussing it, were not happy with a $5 ceiling, but I gather there again you would like to see that adjustable. Is this correct?
Mr. Nelson answered:
Right, either through an escalator clause which would, in turn, take into consideration the cost of production; for example, if the cost of production went up 20 per cent in a year, both the floor and the ceiling ought to go up 20 per cent, or a review aspect in it.
That is what I am asking for in this amendment. Although I could not amend the bill to put in an indexing clause which the Federation of Agriculture wanted, as stated in its very able brief to the committee outlining their point of view, I am suggesting that if the minister had to report to the House of Commons on how much the cost of production went up each year, attention would be focused on the plight of the farmer and members of parliament would bring attention to the need to adjust the bill to compensate for any increase in the cost of production.
The minister stated that the $3.25 floor price is actually the world price. It can be argued that the world price is a few cents below the $3.25 which is the fixed price the Canadian miller would have to pay for Canadian wheat. The minister said in committee that while that price took into consideration the cost of production, the cost of production was not necessarily used in establishing the $3.25. It is immaterial to argue whether it does or does not take into account the cost of production, because we realize that in these inflationary times eventually costs will exceed that floor price.
I think it was generally agreed by all farm organizations that the base price should at least take into consideration the cost of production. The Federation of Agriculture, in their brief to the committee, stated that point quite clearly as recorded in committee proceedings No. 5. The federation stated that since the guaranteed price was set in September of 1973, farm input costs have gone up 14.73 per cent. They estimated that taking an average for the whole of Canada of about 13 per cent of the $3.25, and adding that to the floor price, you will get the base price for 1975 of $3.67. They believe that the base price should at all times include the cost of production. They figure that for 1975 the price should be $3.67.
Surely all we are stating in this amendment is that it should be publicly noted by the minister that the Canadian Wheat Board, whose business it is to know the cost of production of wheat, because they are designated as the major handling agency for western Canada in the Wheat Board area, should assess the cost of production, report to parliament on it and then the onus would be on parliament to adjust the legislation. The amendment moved by the hon. member for Assiniboia does not do much, in my view-or, I am certain, in the view of many farm organizations. It does not make public the cost of production. If the cost of production was made public, everybody would be clearly aware of the responsibility of the minister and of parliament to adjust prices so that farmers could stay in business and continue to produce wheat.
The minister can talk all he likes about the price of wheat going above $5 a bushel, but we all know that costs to the farmers are going up rapidly. We can all remember a few years ago the old cry of farm organizations about the cost-price squeeze and we can foresee it happening again
May 7, 1975

in the years ahead. We hear talk of shortages of gas in Canada and increased oil prices because of Canada's becoming very shortly a net importer of oil. We are not farming in what some people like to refer to as the good old days when we fed our horses a little oats which gave them the energy to pull the plow. We grew our crops with horse power, but we now farm with highly mechanized agricultural implements such as tractors which burn diesel fuel, gas or propane. All farm implements burn a considerable amount of fuel, and fuel costs will more than likely increase unless someone can find a major supply of cheap energy from somewhere other than the OPEC countries.
It is foolish to think that we should tie farmers down for seven years with no escalating clause and no publicly recognized indicator as to how much farm cost will go up. My amendment only suggests that there should be public acknowledgement that those costs will go up, and that the onus is on the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board, whoever that might be in 1977, 1978 or 1979. There will certainly be a new minister after 1978. I would like to think there might be one before that. However, the onus should be on that person to consider those costs which have increased and will continue to increase. Even if we contain inflation, energy costs will more than likely go up as we become a net importer of oil. I put no value on the amendment moved in committee, and I urge the House to accept my amendment. It does not change the legislation; it just makes the minister report to the House the findings of the Canadian Wheat Board on cost of production.
One can read the 1973-74 annual report of the Canadian Wheat Board. It is a very nice, blue document which pertains to the field of agriculture. There is on it a beautiful picture. When I first became a member of parliament this report was referred to the agricultural committee every year. In recent years the government has had to be badgered in order to have a thorough study of the report in the agricultural committee. Nowhere does it suggest that production costs have increased. Nowhere does it deal with the aspect of how much the cost of wheat production has increased. It deals with the total world population and the growth of world production of wheat. It deals with countries we compete against such as Australia and Argentina and their possible production capacity. It deals with importing countries on the continents of North America, Asia, and so on. It deals with feed grain production in the United States and in Canada.
The report deals at length with international wheat agreements. I have nothing against international wheat agreements. Even in international wheat agreements of the past few years there has always been room for the price to fluctuate and move up if there was demand and if the costs of producing countries went up. Of course, if the price did not move up, there would be less and less wheat in the world and more and more people going hungry.
My amendment places greater onus on the Wheat Board to analyse the cost of production. It places greater responsibility on the minister to report those costs to the House. Then, of course, it is up to parliament to assess those costs and perhaps at a future time to adjust Bill C-19 accordingly.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to add a few words to those of the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) in support of his motion, because in the committee I originally moved some amendments with the same idea in mind. Farmers are receiving a bad deal from this government. I have pointed out on various occasions that farmers simply do not trust the minister responsible for the Wheat Board, although at every turn they find it is not only the minister himself; he is simply running true to form as far as any Liberal government is concerned. This has always been the pattern when dealing with Canadian farmers, but we notice it particularly with regard to grain because everyone is aware that grain is one of the great commodities we have for sale. Many of us are dependent on the sale of that commodity for our livelihood.
At one time there was what was known as the British wheat agreement. That agreement was signed by another Liberal government back in 1945 to 1950. At that time there was a "have regard" clause. I merely bring this out because the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale) squirmed and turned in committee after I proposed an amendment which I thought dealt with the matter adequately. There was a rush and a scurry on the part of the Liberal members who were wondering how in the world they could take the credit away from me at that time. They had consultations because my amendment was to appear before theirs. They did not know how to get around that. They had the same idea as I did, but they were not prepared to give me credit for it.
Be that as it may, it turned out that the committee voted on my amendment first. Naturally, it was turned down for no other reason than that it came from a member of the opposition-as though they have any priority on ideas! However, the motion introduced by the hon. member for Assiniboia was dealt with but it is so wishy-washy, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Crowfoot, that it really leaves us with nothing. It leaves us with nothing except a vague reference to a law. It does nothing with regard to pointing out the facts in relation to the cost of production, because at that particular time under the British wheat agreement there was a "have regard" clause. There may be some who remember that clause. There are perhaps very few members who were in the House at that time. Certainly I was not here, but I remember the debate very clearly. At that time, thanks to the Liberal government's lack of foresight, the western farmer lost something like $500 million or $600 million. At that time, the government said that the British would have regard to the cost of grain, that they would take that into account and perhaps pay more if the world price became higher.
As it turned out, the world price of grain dropped tremendously after the war, and countries that were not tied into that type of agreement were getting high prices. Canada was tied to the agreement, however. The present minister looks back on the pages of history in order to follow the pattern of the Liberal Party, so now he is tying us to a fixed price for seven years. Of course, we all know that the cost of production will go up. But what recourse do we have? We cannot introduce an amendment to ask for a higher price, so we ask that the facts be revealed to

the public. It is our opinion that the Canadian public will deal more honestly and fairly with the demands of western farmers than this government, if all the facts are known to them. We already have a Food Prices Review Board. What we are asking for now is a cost-price review board. The Wheat Board has an accounting system and a computer all set up and could take care of the accounting involved.
I really think, Mr. Speaker, that the minister should be required to report to parliament on the cost of production. What we need is a truth squad to go out into the country and determine what the price is. At the moment the minister believes that the $5 price is high enough. I am sure he will have no hesitation in saying a year from now that the bill presented under the two-price system is a good one. We want the minister to be brave enough to tell the western farmer a year from now that his cost of production has not gone up, or has gone up. If he can tell a farm audience, "We paid $5 for seven years", then I want him to stand in this House each year until 1980 pointing, on the one hand, to the $5 ceiling and, on the other hand, to the way the government has managed the cost of production factor. If the government has done its work well and the cost of production has gone down, by 1980 he will be able to say to the farmers, "I gave you $5 and your cost of production has gone down." I would like the minister to do that every year, Mr. Speaker.
After the bill was in committee, I believe the hon. member for Assiniboia complained that some opposition members had filibustered and found fault with it. Well, I am finding fault with it right now, Mr. Speaker. I believe the cost of production will go up. The minister may not believe that, but if he feels so strongly about it he should accept this amendment. If he is confident that the bill is valid now, and will still be valid by 1980, he should accept the amendment. The minister would find a truth squad a valuable instrument to investigate other areas. If the Food Prices Review Board is able to check the cost of food and determine whether anybody is ripping off the consumer, then a parallel case could be made for a cost-price review board.
I hope this House will support the amendment. I hope that two years from now the minister will be brave enough to come before the House and give us the facts, instead of hiding behind unreliable statistics. The relevant statistics are already in the hands of the Canadian Wheat Board, and that is where the minister should look for his information.

Mr. Speaker, I just want to say quickly that we feel we can support this amendment. It will not do any harm, but it might do some good. Some hon. members expressed fears that the amendment might make the Canadian Wheat Board unhappy and place on it the burden of hiring additional staff to produce a statistical analysis on this scale. In the end, of course, the cost would come out of the pockets of the farmers through Wheat Board funds. If the amendment were to pass, however, I think the Wheat Board could use information from Statistics Canada, the Department of National Revenue, universities, research groups and farm management groups.

I like the fact that the amendment calls for the report to be made to parliament. It may well be that the minister will report to parliament following his annual review in any case although nothing in the legislation says that he must. I do not think the amendment would impose any extraordinary requirements on the Wheat Board. If it meant it would have to put in a computer and hire several hundred more people to do the statistical analysis, of course that would be a duplication of effort and a waste of time and money. I think this amendment could be helpful, Mr. Speaker; I do not see how it could be harmful, and I think the minister should accept it and save time in getting his bill through.

subtopic: TWO-PRICE WHEAT ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR PAYMENTS FOR WHEAT PRODUCED AND SOLD IN CANADA FOR HUMAN CONSUMPTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I have listened to interesting comments from both sides of the House on a useful and important bill, Bill C-19, which has been before parliament since last fall, although the mechanics of the program have been in place somewhat longer. Its principles of operation are well known to members of the House who are interested in this subject, and well known particularly to western farmers who, as you know, are most interested in this legislation.
As the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) has pointed out on other occasions, members of this House of all political parties, members of farm organizations across western Canada and, I suspect, of other parts of Canada as well, have made representations about the need in this country for a two-price system for wheat. We saw a proposal of that kind presented to parliament last fall in specific statutory form. We hope soon to see final approval of it.
Let me deal with some misconceptions about this legislation, misconceptions made evident by the amendment which is now before the House. The impression has been conveyed by members opposite speaking on Bill C-19-I hope the impression has been conveyed from a mistaken notion and has not been conveyed deliberately-that this legislation deals with some kind of pegged or fixed price, with a price which will be there for seven years, without room for variation. That, clearly, is not so. The very attractiveness of the legislation lies in the fact that it does not provide for a pegged price, although I suppose a pegged price in Canada is acceptable if it is above the going world price, and that was the situation for some time before this legislation came forward. When you come to the other situation in which the international price is the high price, you cannot talk about a pegged price that is going to to be fully adequate and reasonable over a period of time.
The legislation provides for a price range. It is a useful and good price range and we should look at the parameters of that range as set out by the minister earlier this afternoon. It is a range that is fair and reasonable in the circumstances. Certainly, when it was first established in September, 1973, it was broadly heralded as one that was fair, reasonable and good, and one that exceeded our wildest expectations for grain prices, even for the longer term, just a few months before that range was established. Let us consider what has happened to the price since the beginning of this exercise. Since the Standing Committee on Agriculture finished working on this bill in January or
May 7, 1975

early February, we have seen demonstrated the real value of this kind of arrangement for domestic wheat sold in Canada, as prices have been coming down.
Nobody in this House is happy with that prospect, because we all know what it means in terms of the incomes of western grain and wheat producers and a lot of other producers across the country. Although we are quite optimistic and hopeful that prices in future will continue to be strong, that prices in the rest of the decade will be high for Canadian grain producers, we must face the prospect, unhappily, that prices could and at some stage no doubt will begin to drop. This is borne out by history, unfortunately. So the price range established by this legislation has proved to be a reasonable and realistic one if you consider it from the point of view of the maximum figure which is set at $5 for hard wheat.
On the other side of the coin, some useful opinions were expressed about floor prices. Perhaps one of the most educated and useful opinions which one should consider is that expressed by the chief commissioner of the Canadian Wheat Board, Mr. Vogel, who appeared before the Standing Committee on Agriculture and was questioned strenuously by hon. members on the very point I am making. Mr. Vogel appeared before the committee on November 14 last and his remarks are recorded in issue No. 7 of the proceedings of that committee, on page 26. After dealing with some of the questions I raised and after mentioning the $5 price, Mr. Vogel said, as recorded on that page in the committee minutes:
However, I think it is not correct to ignore the other part of the program which was important to us and that is the guarantee at $3.25 which we do not have on the export market-
Lower on the same page Mr. Vogel is reported as having said:
-I will tell you that as a board we regard the $3.25 as a meaningful figure.
I think it is useful to record that opinion from one who is clearly an expert in the uncertain game of trying to assess where grain prices will go from time to time. He indicated what the realistic expectations of grain producers are if they want to assess their prospects over the longer term. Clearly, the bill is useful in that it provides not for a pegged level of price but for a range of prices. We have, in addition, the amendment which was passed by the committee and presented by government members after it had been thoroughly discussed by committee members. I am referring to clause 5(3) which provides specifically for a review procedure, not in 1977 or some later date but every year. I think that would be a useful exercise, and that amendment by itself makes the amendment now before the House unnecessary.
For the benefit of hon. members who may not be aware of the language of the amendment as adopted by the Standing Committee on Agriculture, I shall read it. The new clause 5(3) reads:
The minister shall, on an annual basis and in consultation with the producers, review the provisions of this act and all related regulations enacted by the governor in council, with a view to making such recommendations to the governor in council as are appropriate in the light of prevailing costs of production of wheat and returns to producers.

It is an all-encompassing amendment which will achieve the objectives hon. members opposite have been urging on the House most of this afternoon.

We are talking about a contract, or an arrangement if you like, the duration of which is to be until 1980. Periodically, we should look at it to ensure that in all circumstances, from the point of view of cost of production and the point of view of total return to producers, the arrangement is fair, reasonable and serves the best interests of this country and, of course, of grain producers who are particularly affected by this legislation.
The members of the Standing Committee on Agriculture did not rush their consideration of this matter. We heard excellent witnesses from farm organizations. At this point I will commend hon. members opposite who came forward in the first place with the suggestion that farm organizations and others should be invited to present their views. That was a useful and constructive idea made by members of opposition parties. As I said, we heard witnesses who presented useful testimony and all who took part in this debate referred to the things they said. After that, and after we had discussed this matter among ourselves, members of the committee on my side of the House felt that the basic argument was well taken and that we had to provide for some ongoing mechanism to take into account changes which might occur from time to time in costs of production and in other circumstances which might affect the effectiveness of the program.
We therefore proposed a review mechanism, but we specifically declined to propose a rigid indexing system. I think the comments made to the committee by the president of the Palliser Wheat Growers' Association, Mr. Nelson, are important. He pointed out that indexing is all very well and good and would at least partly compensate for increases in a farmer's cost of production, but that a host of other factors need to be taken into account between now and 1980, and indexing could not do that. He suggested that an annual review by the minister would be the best way to take these factors into account. These factors might involve cost of production changes or any other changes which might bear upon this legislation.
I think we on my side of the House and, I suspect, hon. members opposite as well, found a good deal of merit in what Mr. Nelson had to say, and we suggested the amendment which is now in the legislation and which I submit largely eliminates the necessity for the amendment presently before us and recently moved by the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner).
As we come to the conclusion of our discussion on this legislation, I want to commend one member of the opposition in particular who participated very actively in the deliberations on Bill C-19. He is not in his place today but I know these remarks will come to his attention. I refer to the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn). Once the amendment had been presented to the committee for consideration, that member took it upon himself to contact at least some of the farm organizations that had appeared before us previously. He asked them to comment

on the amendment the committee was considering; the amendment I read into the record a few moments ago.
It is interesting to see the reactions that came back; they are part of the official record of the committee proceedings. All members of the committee have copies of the letters which came from the various organizations. A reply was received from the Ontario Wheat Producers' Marketing Board. The letter is from Mr. K. A. Standing, general manager of the board, and it reads as follows;
My board have reviewed the proposed amendment to Bill C-19 entitled "Annual Review by Minister".
This board is in accordance with the proposed amendment, and I would appreciate advice on the destiny of the amendment and the bill.
That is clearly an endorsement from that organization. We received a reply from the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool. In his remarks earlier today, the minister commented on what the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool had to say about the amendment. I will read a paragraph of the reply from Mr. Turner, president of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool. In his testimony he clearly opted for the more rigid and less flexible indexing approach. In his letter, he said:
The above amendment, while not specifically committing the government to adjustment of the guarantee and/or the subsidy according to an index of farm input costs, at least recognizes the principle and provides opportunity for annual review.
We also have a reaction from the president of United Grain Growers Limited. The letter is rather lengthy. Mr. Runciman included a copy of some useful remarks he delivered in a speech. I will read the first two paragraphs of his letter to the committee:
The directors of United Grain Growers are most pleased to have the cost of production factor entered as an amendment to Bill C-19.
This is a good amendment and, on behalf of UGG's members, allow me to compliment the Standing Committee on Agriculture for moving it.
From that survey of opinion, which was initiated by the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar, we see a general approval of the kind of amendment that is in the legislation at the moment. It is clearly acknowledged that certain of the farm organizations that appeared before us would like to have seen in the legislation a very inflexible and specific indexing factor. However, for the reasons I discussed earlier, that particular idea did not commend itself to most members of the Standing Committee on Agriculture. I urge the same arguments this afternoon upon members of this House as we come to a final decision on this matter.
I wish to make some comment on certain remarks made during the course of this debate regarding testimony given before the standing committee by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. I think the members of the committee will agree that, like all the groups, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture made a very useful and informative presentation. I think it would be useful for the committee and indeed this House if all members would adopt a rather more consistent attitude with regard to the kind of advice that from time to time comes forward from farm organizations. I say this particularly in connection with advice we have received from the Canadian Federation of Agriculture because they have been singled out by members opposite for consideration in today's debate.

It is important to consider their representations with some consistency. In the course of this debate, members opposite have spoken very highly about what the Canadian Federation of Agriculture have to say. It is quite proper that they should do so because the Canadian Federation of Agriculture presented a very useful brief to the committee on that point. However, this House should demand that hon. members be consistent.
I recall the remarks made in the past week or so by members opposite with regard to another piece of legislation, Bill C-41. The message was just the opposite, that we should not be relying upon the farm organizations and the commentaries they bring forward but, rather, we should circumvent them and address ourselves almost exclusively to the farmers. I do not think the Canadian Federation of Agriculture or any other duly elected farm organization would appreciate that suggestion.
My only plea is for consistency. It is an important principle that we should not treat the advice and counsel of farm groups favourably when it suits our purposes and unfavourably when it does not. It is very important that wherever possible we talk to the individual producers in western Canada or wherever they may be found in this country. However, it is also important to consult with and discuss policy proposals with organizations and groups. Let us do it on all occasions in both directions, not simply in one direction when it is convenient and in another when it may be particularly handy.
I am pleased to note that this government has a high regard for the expressions of individual farmer opinion which come forward to us from time to time. This minister in particular, the minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board, has repeatedly sought direct advice from individual farmers both formally and informally. I think of the formal occasions when he has sought that advice in the manner of a vote or poll. I think of the original vote on the two-price wheat program and the rapeseed marketing plebiscite. Then, there was the recent vote to elect the advisory committee of the Canadian Wheat Board. There have been many informal consultations, too, directly with producers in connection with such things as the stabilization plan, the feed grains policy, grains transportation and other very important issues.
In addition to those consultations between this government and individual producers, directly one to one, this government has demonstrated a high and consistent regard for the counsel and advice of farm organizations duly elected to represent the interests of farmers across the country. I plead that we in this House and elsewhere treat their recommendations with some consistency.
In my view, the basic point is that the amendment of the hon. member for Crowfoot is not necessary. I believe that Bill C-19, with the review procedure-and it is very important that it be in there-is adequate to deal with the situation. We have the obligation of an annual review. The bill as it stands should now enjoy speedy passage; it does not need the additional requirement of the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Crowfoot.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief. We have just had a reiteration of platitudes about the Liberal Party's agricultural policy.
May 7, 1975

They are platitudes, and platitudes only: they produce nothing. Let us look at the platitudes which emanated from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) as an election gimmick. Let us look at the losses suffered by the hog growers in the Atlantic area. Let us look at the cost of the provincial government's stepping in to fill a federal vacuum. A review by the minister will be reflected in every piece of agricultural legislation that we have and in every approach by the government to agriculture. It has finally been decided by an interdepartmental committee, or by a multidepartmental committee, that agriculture is no longer number one. The primary consideration is the politics of the situation, which means that the individual farmer is not given the priority that he deserves.
I submit that the responsibility being placed at this moment in time in the hands of the minister leaves agriculture in the hands of an urban-oriented cabinet which has shown a complete lack of comprehension of the needs of agriculture in all its phases. I will be eating the bread that comes from the wheat that comes from the west; and what this bill does is to ensure that if the international price of wheat goes up, the farmers will lose income: if the international price of wheat goes down, the farmers will then sell on the international market. So the farmer loses either way. The referral structure that has been set up leaves the farmers, as I say, in the hands of an urban-oriented government which has not served, cannot serve, and has no intention of ever serving agriculture as an industry of importance in this country.
